  output$arrestTable <- renderTable({
    processed_arrests()
  })

text:
Google Flu Trends (GFT) sought to detect surges of flu about one to two weeks brefore CDC, based on searches associated with this disease. The model in the beginning followed the CDC data very closely and was very successful. However, the expectation of continuously representing the data with accuracy never became real. GFT did not detect the 2009 H1N1 pandemic and overstimaed the incidence of flu by more than 199 weeds, and predicted more than double the medical appointments recorded by CDC for the 2012-2 seasons.
The failure is supposed to be due to a few factors. The “big data rubris” is the false presumption that big data can ultimately replace traditional monitoring. Google searches may reflect the concern of users regarding the sickness but not the sickness itself. Also, Google keeps changing its algorithms continuously, which must have caused relevant change to the way data is collected and classified. Also, one of the major problmes is that Google was not transparent and never published the terms it used for prediction, making it harder for researchers to validate the consistency of the method.
One example based on my own professional background as a former public sector auditor, is that our whitleblower line received a massive number of manifestations everyday, but most of them were not useful for auditing and fraud detection since most of the files were just citizens complaining about the government or services providade, never giving any useful information on whether there was some kind of fraud, where it was happening, who performed it etc. We had big data, but the data and its collection procedures were not designed to model the data according to our analytical needs.




In my understanding, overfitting occurs whenever a model learns not only the pattern but also the noice of the data in the training dataset. It is good to describe the current data, but bad to predict new ones. Overparametrization is when the model has so many tentative parameters that almost any series can be explained. GFT shows both concepts. With so many parameters, some terms will inevitably correlate with flu by chance. The model ends up trying to explain even what should not be explained.




The lecture titled Data Visualization and data Science, by Hadley Wickham, discussed the importance of visualizing data in any modern data workflow. Wickham addresses the data analysis cycle (loading data, cleansing data, transofrming, visualizing, modeling and reporting) and emphasizes that data viz should not only be used for final reporting but it is a crucial stage for exploratory analysis itself. It allows for the user to find patterns and anomalies, and to see the strucuture of the data that can not be seen from tabular data. Ascombe’s quartet is a classic example of it.
He also discussed the importance of the availability of tools such as R and the Tidyverse and Ggplot2 libraries, that are efficient and easy to implement, which relieves the cognitive toll on analysts, allowing for closer focus on problem resolution instead of worrying about handlingthe software and other implementations issues.

Exercise 2
Using the dataset mtcars

df <- mtcars


a) Set up the canvas

par() sets global graphical parameters (screen layout, margins, default colors) that apply to all plots drawn afterward, until you change them again.


plot.new()                             # opens a blank canvas
#plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10))
box()









box() draws a frame around the plotting area


par(mfrow = c(1, 2))   # splits the "screen" into 1 row, 2 columns
plot.new()
box()
plot.new()# opens a blank canvas
box()









axis() manually draws the axes (tick marks and labels) on a specific side of the plot


par(mfrow = c(1, 2))   # splits the "screen" into 1 row, 2 columns
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10))
box()
axis(1)
axis(2)
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10))
box()
axis(1)
axis(2)










b) Draw whole plots
hist() draws a histogram, showing the frequency distribution of a numeric variable.

hist(mtcars$wt)








boxplot() draws a box plot, showing the summary (median, quartiles, outliers) of a variable, and can compare groups.

boxplot(mtcars$mpg)








pie() draws a pie chart, showing the proportion of each category within a total.

pie(table(mtcars$cyl))








persp() draws a 3D surface, showing how a matrix of values (height z over an x-y grid) is represented in space.

persp(volcano)










c) Add to an existing plot
points() adds extra points to an existing plot, without erasing what was already drawn.

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
points(mtcars$wt[mtcars$cyl == 8], mtcars$mpg[mtcars$cyl == 8],
       col = "red", pch = 19)   # highlights the 8-cylinder cars in red








lines() adds a line (connecting points) to an existing plot.

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
lines(lowess(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg), col = "blue")   # adds a trend line










d) Annotate
text() adds free-standing text inside the plotting area, at specific coordinates.

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
text(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg, labels = rownames(mtcars), pos = 3, cex = 0.6)








mtext() adds text in the plot margin (outside the plotting area), controlling which side/line of the margin receives the text.

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
text(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg, labels = rownames(mtcars), pos = 3, cex = 0.6)
mtext("Weight vs. Fuel Consumption — mtcars", side = 3, line = 1)








legend() draws a legend explaining what each color/symbol in the plot represents.

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg, col = as.factor(mtcars$cyl), pch = 19)
text(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg, labels = rownames(mtcars), pos = 3, cex = 0.6)
mtext("Weight vs. Fuel Consumption — mtcars", side = 3, line = 1)
legend("topright", legend = c("4 cyl", "6 cyl", "8 cyl"),
       col = 1:3, pch = 19)








names() is not a graphical function — it reads or sets names (of vector elements, data frame columns, etc.), making it part of data preparation rather than plotting.

names(mtcars)              # shows the column names

[11] "carb"

text:
2a. One summit, two kinds of text

2a(i). The public: tweets
Reading the archived tweets and describ them in four ways: (1) the most frequent words, (2) which hashtags appear together, (3) which accounts are mentioned together, (4) a Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA).
(1) Frequency

summit <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datageneration/datamethods/master/textanalytics/summit_11162021.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE)
c(tweets = nrow(summit), share_retweets = mean(summit$is_retweet))

        tweets share_retweets 
  1.452000e+04   6.222452e-01 

# corpus -> tokens -> dfm (keeps #hashtags and @mentions for the networks)
twt_dfm <- summit |>
  corpus(text_field = "text") |>
  tokens(remove_punct = TRUE, remove_url = TRUE, remove_symbols = TRUE, remove_numbers = TRUE) |>
  dfm()

# (1) Frequent words: ordinary words only (no stop words, hashtags or mentions)
twt_words <- dfm_remove(twt_dfm, c(my_stop, "#*", "@*"))
twt_freq  <- textstat_frequency(twt_words, n = 25)
ggplot(twt_freq, aes(frequency, reorder(feature, frequency))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#08519c") +
  labs(title = "Most frequent words in the summit tweets", x = "Frequency", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()








(2) and (3) Networks.

# Network of the 50 most used features that match a pattern ("#*" or "@*")
plot_net <- function(pattern, min_freq, colour) {
  d   <- dfm_select(twt_dfm, pattern)
  top <- names(topfeatures(d, 50))
  print(head(top, 10))                                   # the most used ones
  fcm(d) |>
    fcm_select(top) |>
    textplot_network(min_freq = min_freq, edge_color = colour, edge_alpha = 0.8, edge_size = 1)
}
plot_net("#*", min_freq = 50, colour = "#08519c")    # (2) hashtags used in the same tweet

 [6] "#americans"   "#coronavirus" "#fentanyl"    "#xi"          "#us"         








plot_net("@*", min_freq = 20, colour = "firebrick")  # (3) accounts mentioned in the same tweet

 [6] "@nwadhams"    "@phelimkine"  "@nahaltoosi"  "@nba"         "@washwizards"









(4) Latent Semantic Analysis.

twt_lsa <- textmodel_lsa(twt_words, nd = 4)
# The 10 words with the largest loading (in absolute value) on each dimension
top10 <- apply(abs(twt_lsa$features), 2, \(x) paste(names(sort(x, decreasing = TRUE))[1:10], collapse = ", "))
data.frame(dimension = 1:4, top_words = top10)

Interpreting 2a(i).
The 14,520 tweets (62% of them retweets) are dominated by the names of the two leaders and the format of the event: the most frequent words are biden, xi, summit, virtual, president, jinping, china, chinese. The hashtag network shows two clusters: one around the leaders and the bilateral agenda (#china, #biden, #xijinping, #fentanyl, #coronavirus, #taiwan) and one around human rights (#uyghurgenocide, #tibetans, #humanrights), which the official agenda barely names. The mention network links official and media accounts (@potus, @joebiden, @politico, journalists) and also a separate cluster formed by basketball player Enes Kanter and NBA accounts, a protest against China that happened in the same days. The first LSA dimension simply collects the general summit vocabulary; the others pick up narrower threads, such as Xi calling Biden an “old friend” and references to Russia and Ukraine. Because many tweets are retweets, frequent words partly reflect a few messages copied many times.


2a(ii). The government: Compilation of Presidential Documents

searching GovInfo for all CPD documents that contain “Xi Jinping” since Biden’s inauguration and downloadig them, keeping a log and a manifest; (2) read every mention of Xi with the words around it (kwic()); (3) use keyness to find the words that distinguish the Biden documents from the Trump documents.

Step 1. Collect. Search, download (with a log), convert to text, and write the manifest. GovInfo returns results in pages of 100, so the search function keeps asking for the next page while pages come back full. Documents are saved in data-raw/ (ignored by Git); each one is assigned to an administration by its date (Trump from 20 January 2025).

# Search GovInfo, following every page of results
search_govinfo <- function(query) {
  out <- list(); offset <- "*"                          # "*" = first page
  while (!is.null(offset)) {
    res <- request("https://api.govinfo.gov/search") |>
      req_url_query(api_key = govinfo_key) |>           # >>> API KEY (from .Renviron)
      req_body_json(list(query = query, pageSize = 100, offsetMark = offset)) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()
    out    <- c(out, res$results)
    offset <- if (length(res$results) == 100) res$offsetMark else NULL   # next page, if any
  }
  tibble(package_id = map_chr(out, "packageId"),
         title      = map_chr(out, "title"),
         date       = as.Date(map_chr(out, "dateIssued")))
}

# The query: CPD collection + exact phrase in the full text + from 20 Jan 2021 to today
cpd_query <- sprintf('collection:(CPD) AND "Xi Jinping" AND publishdate:range(2021-01-20,%s)', Sys.Date())
cpd <- search_govinfo(cpd_query) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2021-01-20")) |>
  mutate(file = file.path(raw_dir, paste0(package_id, ".htm")),
         url  = paste0("https://api.govinfo.gov/packages/", package_id, "/htm"))
n_found <- nrow(cpd)

# Download each document (skipped if already on disk); a failure is logged, not fatal
cpd$status <- map2_chr(cpd$url, cpd$file, \(url, file) {
  if (file.exists(file)) return("already downloaded")
  Sys.sleep(0.5)                                         # be polite to the API
  tryCatch({
    request(url) |> req_url_query(api_key = govinfo_key) |> req_perform(path = file)  # >>> API KEY
    "ok"
  }, error = \(e) paste("failed:", conditionMessage(e)))
})
n_failed <- sum(grepl("failed", cpd$status))
write_csv(transmute(cpd, package_id, url, status, time = Sys.time()),   # log (URL without the key)
          file.path(log_dir, "cpd_xi_download_log.csv"))

# Plain text + administration, then the manifest (published; the documents are not)
cpd <- cpd |>
  filter(file.exists(file)) |>
  mutate(text  = map_chr(file, \(f) html_text2(read_html(f))),
         admin = if_else(date >= as.Date("2025-01-20"), "Trump", "Biden"))
write_csv(transmute(cpd, package_id, title, date, admin, n_chars = nchar(text),
                    source = paste0("https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/", package_id)),
          file.path(log_dir, "cpd_xi_manifest.csv"))
count(cpd, admin)

Step 3. Keyness. Keyness compares the relative frequency of every word in a target group with a reference group (chi-square test). Large positive values are typical of the target (Trump); large negative values are typical of the reference (Biden).

2b. US presidential inaugural addresses, 1945 onward

2b(i). Similarities and differences

Any similarities and differences over time and among presidents? Use length, lexical diversity, readability, cosine similarity, and keyness by party.

Using the inaugural corpus that comes with quanteda, keep the addresses from 1945 on, and compare them with five measures. The first three are computed together:

Length: number of words.
Lexical diversity: how varied the vocabulary is. The type-token ratio (TTR = different words / total words) falls automatically as a text gets longer, so the moving-average TTR (MATTR, over windows of 100 words) is used to compare addresses of different lengths.
Readability: Flesch Reading Ease (higher = easier) and Flesch–Kincaid grade level (the US school grade needed to follow the text), both based on sentence length and syllables per word.


inaug      <- corpus_subset(data_corpus_inaugural, Year >= 1945)   # addresses since 1945
inaug_toks <- tokens(inaug, remove_punct = TRUE)
inaug_dfm  <- inaug_toks |> tokens_remove(stopwords("en")) |> dfm()

# One row per address: length, lexical diversity, readability
inaug_info <- docvars(inaug) |>
  mutate(doc = docnames(inaug), n_tokens = ntoken(inaug_toks)) |>
  left_join(textstat_lexdiv(inaug_toks, c("TTR", "MATTR"), MATTR_window = 100),
            by = c("doc" = "document")) |>
  left_join(textstat_readability(inaug, c("Flesch", "Flesch.Kincaid")),
            by = c("doc" = "document"))

# The three measures over time, one panel each (grey line = overall trend)
inaug_info |>
  select(Year, President, Party, Words = n_tokens, `Lexical diversity (MATTR)` = MATTR,
         `Readability (Flesch-Kincaid grade)` = Flesch.Kincaid) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(Year, President, Party)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Year, value)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = Party)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = President, colour = Party), vjust = -0.6, size = 2.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ name, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = party_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_bw()







inaug_info |>
  select(Year, President, Party, n_tokens, TTR, MATTR, Flesch, Flesch.Kincaid) |>
  mutate(across(TTR:Flesch.Kincaid, \(x) round(x, 2)))

Cosine similarity: each address is a vector of word counts; the cosine of the angle between two vectors is 1 when the word use is identical and 0 when the two texts share no words. Words are weighted by tf-idf so that words every address uses (“nation”, “people”) count less.

sim     <- textstat_simil(dfm_tfidf(inaug_dfm), method = "cosine")
sim_mat <- as.matrix(sim)
diag(sim_mat) <- NA        # an address compared with itself (= 1) would flatten the colours

  ggplot(aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#08519c", name = "cosine", na.value = "grey90") +

  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, size = 7), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7))

Keyness by party: words used unusually often by Republican presidents (target, red) compared with Democratic presidents (reference, blue).

party_key <- textstat_keyness(dfm_group(inaug_dfm, Party), target = "Republican")
textplot_keyness(party_key, n = 20, color = c("firebrick", "#08519c")) +
  labs(title = "Inaugural addresses since 1945: Republican (red) vs. Democratic (blue)")








Comments on 2b(i).

Length. Addresses range from 557 words (Roosevelt, 1945, a wartime fourth inauguration) to 2,913 words (Trump, 2025). The fitted line rises slightly over time, but it is pulled down by Roosevelt’s very short wartime address; there is no clear party difference, and length depends more on the president and the moment.
Lexical diversity. The simple TTR is misleading, because it is highest for the shortest address. Once length is corrected with MATTR, the differences are small (roughly between 0.64 and 0.71): presidents differ little in vocabulary richness in this genre.
Readability. Most addresses require between a 7th- and a 12th-grade reading level. The trend over time is weak (the fitted line changes by about -0.1 grades per decade), and the differences come mostly from individual presidents: the easiest address to read is Biden 2021 (grade 5.8), well below all the others, while the hardest is Nixon 1973 (grade 12.3).
Cosine similarity. The most similar pair is 2001-Bush and 2021-Biden, and 5 of the 10 most similar pairs are two addresses by the same president. A president’s vocabulary carries over from the first to the second term; the other close pairs mix parties (for example Bush 2001 and Biden 2021), so similarity does not follow party lines. Overall the cosines are low, because each address is written for its own moment.
Keyness by party. The words that distinguish Republicans are federal, going, seen, government, thank, freedom, country, system; Democrats are distinguished by democracy, change, must, forth, journey, generation, enough, still. The differences are modest (small chi-square values): the ceremonial genre pushes both parties toward the same language.

title: Research
text:
Machine Learning applied to Public Sector Auditing: A case study with data from the department of health of the state of São Paulo, Brazil

Abstract:
Machine Learning (ML), as a field of Artificial Intelligence (AI), has become increasingly popular due to its ease of learning, scalability, and low cost. Both industry and academia have researched useful and feasible ways to apply ML algorithms for practical use in multiple fields, both academic and professional, taking advantage of their ability to learn patterns to predict future variables, classify or group data, and detect anomalous observations. Although the private sector has quickly evolved in studying the application of ML to financial fraud, stock market modeling and financial distress prediction, the application of these techniques in the public sector, namely in public audit, still demands further research for practical use. In this paper, I conduct a review of the current literature on machine learning applications for management-related fields and propose a case study to advance its application to public audit. I identified the Isolation Forest (iForest) algorithm as one of the most effective, scalable, and recognized for detecting anomalies. I applied it to a dataset with expenditure data from the Department of Health of the city of São Paulo, Brazil, and found that the algorithm can be of practical use for anomalous transaction value detection, but ineffective in identifying expenditure misclassification. The paper contributes to the scarce literature on the application of ML to public audit and seeks to promote further investigation for public oversight and improved management.

library(tidycensus) 
library(tigris) 
library(sf) 
library(dplyr) 
library(ggplot2) 
library(readr) 
library(tidyr) 
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)





Run this only once IN THE CONSOLE DO NOT ADD API KEY TO THE SCRIPT

census_api_key("YOUR API KEY HERE", install = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE)

ATTENTION! API KEYS expires quickly. Request a new one whenever needed.




Download a complete list of codes and descriptions available for the 2024 ACS 5-year (“acs5”) and stores it in a table called vars. It is like a data dictionary
The Census Bureau has thousands of variables in the ACS, and each one is identified by a cryptic code like B19013_001 or B17001_002 — nobody memorizes these. load_variables() downloads the full catalog of available variable codes and their human-readable descriptions (like a dictionary or index) and stores it in vars.
This step doesn’t download any actual data about counties, states, income, or poverty numbers. It’s purely a reference table you browse through (you filtered it with grepl(“^B19”, name)) to figure out which exact codes correspond to the concepts you want to study — in your case, median household income and poverty. You use this step once, just to look things up, then you already know the codes you need (B19013_001, B17001_002, B17001_001), which get hardcoded into my_vars in the next part of the script.

vars <- load_variables(2023, "acs5")

Keeps only the rows where the variable name starts with “B19”.

grepl is a text/pattern search (regex), and \^B19 means “starts with B19”.

Variables starting with B19 are all income-related, so this filters the giant dictionary down to just the income variables.

slice_head can also capture the top n rows of each group with group_by()

  dplyr::slice_head(n = 10) 
print(vars)

Now that you know exactly which variable codes you want, get_acs() is the function that actually contacts the Census API and pulls the real numbers for those specific codes, for the specific geography you chose (here, counties in Missouri). This is the step that returns actual estimates and margins of error for real places, plus (because geometry = TRUE) the map boundaries for each county.
But before, let’s set up the paramers for our search.

survey <- "acs5" 
year_acs <- 2024 
state_abbr <- "MO" 
geo_level <- "county" 
my_vars <- c( 
  income = "B19013_001", # median household income 
  pov = "B17001_002", # people below poverty 
  povden = "B17001_001" # poverty universe = denominator 
  )




Let’s now download the data

acs_wide <- get_acs( 
  geography = geo_level, 
  variables = my_vars, 
  state = state_abbr, 
  year = year_acs, 
  survey = survey, 
  geometry = TRUE, 
  # 'wide' for variables in columns 'long' is default for variables in rows 
  output = "wide" 
  )

In R, an object can be more than one thing at the same time:

data.frame means it’s a table
sf means it’s also a spatial object (simple features) because it has a special column storing the geometry
That extra layer is what lets you use geom_sf() in ggplot() to draw maps


class(acs_wide)

[1] "sf"         "data.frame"





The chunk below calculates the poverty rate for each county: it takes the estimated number of people below the poverty line (povE, from B17001_002) and divides it by the total population in the “poverty universe” for that county (povdenE, from B17001_001 — the denominator, i.e., the population this poverty measure applies to). The result is a proportion (for example, 0.15 = 15% of people in that county are below the poverty line).
When you simply divide two numbers that each already have their own margins of error (povM and povdenM), you can’t just divide the margins of error too (povM / povdenM would be wrong). Because povE (people in poverty) is a subset of povdenE (everyone), the two estimates are statistically correlated, and there’s a specific Census Bureau formula for correctly calculating the margin of error of a proportion derived from two other estimates.
moe_prop() is a function from the tidycensus package itself that already implements that official Census formula for you. It takes: - povE — numerator estimate (people in poverty) - povdenE — denominator estimate (total population) - povM — numerator’s MOE - povdenM — denominator’s MOE
And returns the correct MOE for the pov_rate you just calculated.
In practice: without this line, you’d have each county’s poverty rate but no idea how reliable that number is. With pov_moe, you can say, for example, “this county’s poverty rate is 15% ± 3 percentage points” — which is essential for the part of the assignment that asks you to compare areas and check whether their confidence intervals overlap (the “Uncertainty check” deliverable).

acs_wide <- acs_wide %>% 
  mutate(
    pov_rate = povE / povdenE, 
    pov_moe = moe_prop(povE, povdenE, povM, povdenM)
    )

In his paper (1973), Anscombe claims that visualizing data is crucial for statistical analysis. To support his claim, he presented a dataset that generated four different visualizations in which the data displays totally different behaviors, even though the regression summary was exactly the same for all. That illustrates the fact that only by running statistical/mathematical metrics may not be enough for a scientist to understand the underlying nature of data.
In his paper, Anscombe suggested that data that is not linear could be adjusted by applying transformation functions to the x-axis, to the y-axis or both. Today, with libraries such as the scikit-learn library in Python, it is possible to conduct multiple types of transformations not only to linearize data but also to shape the data under several desired statistical distributions.

  {

    y=points[1, "y1"]+sin(points[1, "alfa"]*(pi/180))
    points[1,"x2"]=x
    points[1,"y2"]=y
    data.frame(x1 = x, y1 = y, x2 = NA, y2 = NA,

    points[1, "depth"]=points[1, "depth"]+1

  }
}

plot_anscombe <- function(dataset_num) {
  x_col <- paste0("x", dataset_num)

  mod <- lm(formula, data = anscombe)

    "RSE = ", rse

We can see that the values for the slope, the intercept, the R2 and the RSE are the same for all four models. That reveals that without visualizing the data, an analyst could make serious modeling mistakes. Plotting the data, however reveals that each data set behaves very differently from the others. Data set 2 and data set 4, for example, are clearly nonlinear, which is prohibitive for regressions.

Another way to see the regressions is using confidence intervals. Once again, a different visualization proves that the data sets are different, regardless of the equivalent metrics:

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

data(anscombe)

plot_anscombe <- function(dataset_num) {
  x_col <- paste0("x", dataset_num)
  y_col <- paste0("y", dataset_num)
  formula <- as.formula(paste(y_col, "~", x_col))
  mod <- lm(formula, data = anscombe)
  intercept <- round(coef(mod)[1], 3)
  slope     <- round(coef(mod)[2], 3)
  r2        <- round(summary(mod)$r.squared, 3)
  rse       <- round(summary(mod)$sigma, 3)
  stats_label <- paste0(
    "Intercept = ", intercept, "\n",
    "Slope = ", slope, "\n",
    "R² = ", r2, "\n",
    "RSE = ", rse
  )
  
  # Building confidence bands
  ggplot(anscombe, aes_string(x = x_col, y = y_col)) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, 
                color = "blue", fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_point(fill = "tomato", color = "red", shape = 21, size = 3) +
    annotate("text", x = 3.5, y = 11.5, label = stats_label, 
             hjust = 0, size = 3.2, family = "sans") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(3, 19)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(3, 13)) +
    labs(title = paste("Dataset", dataset_num), x = paste0("x", dataset_num), y = paste0("y", dataset_num)) +
    theme_bw()
}

The two vector formats store drawing instructions instead of pixels, which is why the PDF files are the smallest. The SVG files show the biggest difference between the two systems. Base R’s svg() converts every letter into a drawn outline, while ggsave() writes through the svglite package and keeps the labels as real text. This makes the ggplot2 SVG about 13 times smaller and keeps its text searchable. BMP stores every pixel without compression, so it is about 75 times larger than the PNG of the same image. At quality 90, the JPG is not smaller than the PNG, because a chart has large flat areas of colour that lossless compression already handles well.

The vector formats look the same at any zoom level because the viewer redraws them at the new size. The raster formats only enlarge the pixels that were saved at 300 dpi. PNG, TIFF and BMP look identical to each other because all three are lossless; only the JPG loses information.
